title: The Banaras Hindu University Speech (1916): Confronting the Princes
summary: Surrounded by bejeweled maharajas and colonial governors, Gandhi stunned the gathering by declaring that there was no salvation for India unless the princes stripped themselves of their jewels and identified with the starving peasantry.
keywords: The Banaras Hindu University Speech (1916): Confronting the Princes
full_text:
On February 4, 1916, the royal amphitheater of Banaras Hindu University was ablaze with imperial grandeur.

Seated upon the dais were Viceroy Lord Hardinge, Annie Besant, and the most powerful maharajas and nawabs of princely India—draped in silks, with ropes of pearls and emeralds glinting under the chandeliers.

Invited to speak as an obscure returnee from South Africa, M. K. Gandhi stepped to the lectern.

What followed was an oratorical earthquake that altered Indian history.

Looking directly at the bejeweled monarchs, Gandhi spoke with chilling candor:
"Your Highnesses! My heart is sick with grief at the spectacle before me.
Behold the gorgeous display of jewelry adorning the princes on this stage!
I compare it with the impoverished masses of our country whom I met on my train journeys.
From where did the gold and diamonds in your necklaces originate?
They were wrung from the sweat and blood of the Indian ryot—the impoverished peasant who toils in the scorching sun for a single bowl of rice!

I say plainly to you today:
**There is no salvation for India unless you strip yourselves of these jewels and hold that wealth in sacred trust for your countrymen!**
The freedom of this nation does not reside in your palaces; it resides in the huts of our starving peasantry!"

Annie Besant leaped up in distress: "Stop, Mr. Gandhi! Please stop! This is outrageous!"

Gandhi turned to her calmly: "Madam, I am speaking the bitter truth! If I cannot voice the agony of our people here, I must walk away."

Several maharajas walked off the stage in indignation.

That legendary speech shattered the illusion that Indian freedom could be won by elite aristocrats and transferred the leadership of the nation to the hands of the common people.
moral: Moral leadership demands speaking uncomfortable truths to power, refusing to flatter the wealthy while the poor suffer.
